title: Less Is More: A Minimally Invasive Approach to Anterior Aesthetic Rehabilitation
html:
Written by: Adamo E. Notarantonio, DDS

With the rise of social media, dentistry has never been more visible. Platforms like Instagram and Facebook have flooded our feeds with before-and-after transformations. While this exposure has increased public awareness of what modern dentistry can achieve, it has also fueled a dangerous appetite for immediate results. Too often, cases prioritize speed and dramatic aesthetics over time, patience, and precision. We frequently see full-mouth preparations performed simply to correct malaligned teeth and improve smile aesthetics—all while ignoring underlying health concerns such as airway, sleep, and breathing dysfunction, and without first exploring whether repositioning the teeth orthodontically might be the more appropriate solution.

Case Presentation

A 28-year-old female presented for an aesthetic consultation with a chief complaint of a reverse smile line—specifically, insufficient display of her maxillary anterior teeth and excessive visibility of her mandibular anterior teeth. Figures 1 to 4 represent the full series of diagnostic photographs taken at the initial appointment to evaluate both aesthetic and functional concerns. In Figures 1 and 3 (the full smile and close-up smile, both with teeth apart) the lack of central incisor length and the reverse smile architecture are clearly evident. Figure 2, the repose photograph, demonstrates an excessive display of the lower dentition, which is particularly notable given the patient’s age.

To address this presentation, 2 treatment philosophies were considered.

The first, more aggressive approach, would involve opening the patient’s vertical dimension and adding length to the maxillary anterior teeth to resolve the aesthetic concern, while simultaneously restoring all mandibular posterior teeth to maintain the new vertical. This approach would require treating otherwise healthy, untouched dentition—an unnecessary compromise of tooth structure.

The second, far more conservative option would involve minor orthodontics to intrude and retract the mandibular anterior teeth, followed by restoration of only the maxillary 4 anterior teeth with minimal preparations.

Treatment Planning and Smile Design

Prior to presenting treatment options, a comprehensive dentofacial analysis was performed (Figure 5), along with a 2D digital smile design mockup (Figure 6). The dentofacial analysis provided critical data—tooth proportions, maxillary and mandibular lip dynamics, and interalar width at both smile and repose—to guide the restorative blueprint. After viewing the mockup, the patient immediately responded, “Yeah, that’s what I want.”

Both options were presented and discussed in full. The patient was advised that the preferred approach was the conservative one: limited orthodontics followed by porcelain veneers on the maxillary anterior teeth only. The patient agreed without hesitation. Invisalign (Align Technology) was completed on the mandibular arch exclusively, with the primary objectives of intrusion and retraction of the lower 4 incisors. Upon completion of orthodontic treatment, a new scan was uploaded into the Evident Hub platform (Evident Digital) to convert the 2D smile design into a 3D mockup for use at the preparation appointment.

Preparation Appointment

On the day of preparation, the 3D mockup was seated directly over the patient’s existing anterior teeth for in-mouth approval. Following confirmation, the patient was anesthetized and the maxillary arch was isolated under rubber dam (Nictone) using a split-dam technique. The palatal aspect was sealed with bite registration material (Futar Fast [Kettenbach]).

To ensure the most conservative preparation possible, we used the APT (Aesthetic Pre-evaluative Temporaries) developed by Dr. Galip Gürel, as illustrated in Figures 7 to 9. Incisal depth cuts of 1.5 mm and facial depth cuts of 0.5 mm were used to guide uniform, minimal reduction. Final preparations were completed entirely under rubber dam isolation (Figure 10).

Prior to impression-taking, 00 retraction cord was placed at each preparation, and a refined finish line was established with a high-speed diamond (Figure 11). Given that all margins were at the gingival crest, retraction paste (Expasyl [ACTEON]) was selected over a double-cord technique (Figure 12). Two consecutive final impressions in PVS material were taken to ensure laboratory-quality accuracy (Figure 13). Provisionals were placed using a spot-etch and shrink-wrap technique, followed by trimming, occlusal verification, and polishing (Figure 14).

One week later, the patient returned for provisional approval photographs and digital scans, allowing the laboratory to replicate the provisional contours precisely in the final restorations. Figure 15 captures the provisionals 5 weeks post-insertion. Figures 16 to 18 document the laboratory fabrication process: full-contour pressed lithium disilicate veneers with facial and incisal cutback to introduce translucency and internal optical effects. All laboratory work was completed by Ghaith Sultan, MDT, of Dubai, UAE.

Insertion Appointment

On the day of insertion, the patient was anesthetized, provisionals were removed, and the final restorations were tried in for approval. Following patient sign-off, isolation was established using the Absolute Isolation technique, with individual rubber dam placement across the anterior 6 teeth. The 2 teeth being bonded at any given time were further isolated with accessory B4 clamps (Coltène/Whaledent) for additional soft tissue retraction (Figures 19 and 20).

Each preparation was air-abraded with 27-µm aluminum oxide at 40 PSI using a PrepStart unit (Zest Dental Solutions). Given that all preparations remained entirely within enamel, a total-etch technique was selected, followed by All-Bond Universal (BISCO) as the bonding agent. The 2 central veneers were bonded and cleaned of excess material first, after which the B4 clamps were repositioned to the lateral incisors and the same protocol was followed in sequence.

Figure 21 captures the completed cementation sequence under full rubber dam isolation (Choice 2 [BISCO]). Upon completion, the Absolute Isolation was converted to a split-dam configuration to allow thorough margin finishing. As shown in Figure 22, the presence of hemorrhage beneath the rubber dam confirms the effectiveness of a properly placed thick latex dam in excluding sulcular fluid during a technique-sensitive adhesive protocol. Following dam removal, occlusion was meticulously evaluated in both maximum intercuspation and all excursive movements.

Postoperative Results

One month following insertion, the patient returned for follow-up documentation. The same photographic sequence captured at the initial consultation was repeated to allow direct comparison. Figure 23 presents the full-face, before-and-after smile photograph. Figure 24, the postoperative repose image, shows a marked reduction in mandibular anterior tooth display and appropriate visibility of the restored maxillary incisors—a direct contrast to Figure 2. Figures 25 and 26 illustrate the post-op retracted teeth-apart view and the final close-up smile, respectively.

At the conclusion of the post-op appointment, the patient participated in a celebration photo session in the historic areas surrounding the practice in Huntington, NY (Figure 27).

CONCLUSION

The Imperative of Minimally Invasive Thinking

This case illustrates what is perhaps the most important principle in modern restorative dentistry: the best preparation is often the least preparation. In a specialty increasingly shaped by social media aesthetics and patient demand for rapid transformation, clinicians must serve as the voice of biological reason—advocating for treatment approaches that respect tooth structure, honor the longevity of the natural dentition, and address the underlying etiology rather than masking it with restorations.

Minimally invasive dentistry is not a limitation—it is a philosophy. When orthodontics can move teeth to where they belong, we should move them. When preparations can be kept within enamel, they should be. When fewer teeth can be treated to achieve the desired outcome, that is the correct treatment plan. In this case, by completing limited mandibular orthodontics prior to any restorative work, we avoided restoring an entire arch of healthy posterior teeth, preserved the patient’s native occlusal vertical dimension, and limited our restorative footprint to 4 maxillary veneers—all while achieving a result the patient described as exactly what she had envisioned.

Conservative care is not the easier path. It demands more diagnostic rigor, more interdisciplinary coordination, more patient communication, and more technical precision than simply preparing everything in sight. The APT technique, meticulous rubber dam isolation, and a disciplined adhesive protocol are not shortcuts—they are the infrastructure that makes conservative dentistry predictable and durable. Done well, minimally invasive restorative dentistry not only preserves tooth structure today; it protects the patient’s oral health across a lifetime.

As clinicians, we have an obligation to resist the cultural pressure for instant, dramatic results when a more measured approach will serve the patient better in the long run. The case presented here is proof that when diagnosis drives treatment planning—rather than the desire for a compelling before-and-after—the outcomes are not only beautiful, but they are biologically sound, structurally conservative, and built to last.
